claims.text: Economic development is the sustained improvement in a country's living standards, judged by income per head together with indicators of wellbeing: life expectancy at birth, adult literacy, and the share of households with clean water, electricity and schooling.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: GDP per head divides a country's total output for the year by its population, so it measures average income; two countries with the same total output can sit far apart in output per head where their populations differ, which is why comparisons of development use GDP per head rather than total output.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: GDP per head on its own does not settle a country's level of development: it is an average that may sit high while many households stay poor, and it does not record health, education or access to services, so two countries with close GDP per head may still rank differently on the wider indicators.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Low income per head tends to hold back its own improvement: where incomes are low, households spend most of their income on necessities and governments collect little tax revenue, so spending on schooling, healthcare and clean water tends to be small, and the workers this produces tend to raise output per head slowly in turn.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Productivity is output per worker in a period; differences in productivity, caused by differences in capital, technology, skills, health and the organisation of production, tend to cause differences in income per head, because workers who each produce more can be paid more and generate more tax revenue, which in turn can fund more capital and training.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Where population grows faster than output, GDP per head falls; fast population growth also brings a large share of young dependants, so more income goes on schooling, food and health care and less is saved and invested, while a slowly growing or shrinking population faces a shrinking workforce instead.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: The primary sector extracts natural resources (farming, fishing, forestry, mining), the secondary sector turns materials into goods (manufacturing, construction), and the tertiary sector provides services; low-income countries tend to have a large share of workers in the primary sector, often in low-productivity farming, high-income countries tend to have most workers in the tertiary sector, and as countries develop, workers tend to move from the primary towards the secondary and tertiary sectors.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: A country that depends heavily on the primary sector tends to have lower and less stable income per head, because output per farm worker is often low and the prices of crops and minerals swing on world markets; larger secondary and tertiary sectors tend to bring higher productivity and wages, though a well-managed resource sector can support high income, as in Norway.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Low income limits saving, because households spend most of their income on necessities; low saving leaves banks few funds to lend for investment in machinery, buildings and infrastructure, so the capital stock grows slowly and productivity and income stay low, while high saving and investment, as in South Korea during its period of rapid growth, build the capital that raises productivity.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Education raises the skills of the workforce, so countries with better-educated workers tend to have higher productivity, attract firms producing higher-value goods and services, and earn higher incomes; where many children leave school early, workers have fewer skills, lower productivity and lower wages.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Better health care keeps workers fit, cuts working days lost to illness, lengthens life expectancy and helps children learn, so productivity and income tend to be higher; it also lowers infant deaths, after which birth rates tend to fall; poor health care cuts output and earnings and diverts household income to treatment.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.
